g.text: System design — the watermark generator
max seen − 60s, per source, minimum across · naive formula regresses 2x
seed: tools/stream_seed.js · lag 60s · window [12:00, 12:02) = 19
WATERMARK GENERATOR — WHERE IT LIVES AND WHAT IT READS
the generator reads event times and emits one number; nothing else changes
sources (events with event time)
2 sources here: "a", "b"
watermark generator
per source: max seen − 60s · across sources: the minimum
window assigner
by event time, into 120s windows — unaffected by the watermark
per-window state → trigger/emitter → dashboard
the trigger is the ONLY consumer of the watermark
The assigner does not consult the watermark — bucketing is pure `winOf(e.et)`. Only the TRIGGER reads it.
So a watermark bug cannot put an event in the wrong window. It can only make a window speak too early or too late, which is why its failures look
like wrong totals rather than wrong groupings.
Step 1/4 — the generator sits between the sources and the windows
Worth being precise about the blast radius: the watermark feeds exactly one consumer, the trigger. Windowing is `winOf(e.et)` and never sees it.
That is why a mis-tuned skew produces an under-counted window rather than scattered data — and why "my numbers are low" is the symptom to map back
to this component.
System design — the watermark generator

seed: tools/stream_seed.js · lag 60s · window [12:00, 12:02) = 19
WHY max() IS IN THE FORMULA
row 2 = this event's own time − 60s (naive) · row 3 = max seen − 60s (correct)
id 0
id 1
id 2
id 3
id 4
id 5
id 6
id 7
id 8
none yet
none yet
none yet
none yet
none yet
The naive row regresses 2 times: 12:03:20 → 12:02:40 (−40s) and 12:02:40 → none yet (−170s).
A watermark that moves backwards would RE-OPEN a window that had already been closed and published, so every downstream guarantee collapses.
`max()` is what makes that impossible.
Step 2/4 — the naive formula goes BACKWARDS — twice
Two formulas differing by one function call. `e.et − skew` looks equivalent and is not: it falls back 40s at id 6 and 170s at id 7. Monotonicity
is not a nicety — a backwards watermark un-closes a published window, and nothing downstream is prepared for that.
System design — the watermark generator
max seen − 60s, per source, minimum across · naive formula regresses 2x
seed: tools/stream_seed.js · lag 60s · window [12:00, 12:02) = 19
WHAT THERE IS TO GET WRONG
two independent choices: how big a skew, and whether to track per source
skew bound 60s (the default)
window [12:00, 12:02) publishes 15 at 12:04:06 · 1 late
skew bound 141s (the threshold)
publishes 19 at 12:09:02 · 0 late · 296s slower
one global watermark
claims 12:08:00 at the end — 280s more than source "b" supports
per-source minimum
claims 12:03:20 — safe, and withholds 11, 7
Both settings trade the same pair: latency against the number of events the pipeline will mislabel as late.
Neither has a right answer, and both thresholds (141s, and the 280s gap) were computed from a stream this generator can see in full.
Step 3/4 — the two settings, and their exact thresholds
Two knobs. The skew bound has a threshold of 141s for this window, costing 296s of latency. Per-source tracking is strictly safer and withholds
11, 7 when a source goes quiet. Both thresholds are only computable here because the whole stream is in hand — in production they are guesses, and
the design has to survive them being wrong.
System design — the watermark generator
max seen − 60s, per source, minimum across · naive formula regresses 2x
seed: tools/stream_seed.js · lag 60s · window [12:00, 12:02) = 19
SCOPE
The 60s skew bound is unverifiable from inside the pipeline. Nothing distinguishes "no late events" from "late events we already discarded".
Per-source tracking requires knowing the source set. A source that never appears cannot be waited for, and one that disappears pins the watermark
at 12:03:20 forever without an idleness timeout.
Monotonicity is enforced here by `max()`. A generator that restarts and recomputes from a checkpoint can still emit a lower value than it
published before — this design says nothing about that.
And window [12:08, …) never closes under ANY skew bound in the sweep, because no event ever pushes the watermark past its end.
Step 4/4 — and what the generator does NOT settle
The second and third gaps are the ones that cause production incidents. An idle source with no timeout pins the watermark forever and every window
stops closing — an outage that looks like a stall, not an error. And a restarted generator recomputing from a checkpoint can publish a watermark
below one it already published, which breaks the monotonicity every downstream trigger assumes.
